slides.title: Modern AI Milestones: Watson, AlphaGo, GPTs
slides.text:
Modern AI Milestones: Watson, AlphaGo, GPTs
1. IBM Watson – AI for Question Answering (2011)
What It Did:
IBM Watson was built to compete on the US quiz show Jeopardy!
In 2011, it defeated top human champions Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter.
Technology Behind Watson:
Used DeepQA architecture, combining:
Natural language processing (NLP)
Information retrieval
Machine learning
Statistical reasoning
Could parse complex language, understand puns, and infer answers from vast unstructured data.
Impact:
Marked a leap in machine comprehension and NLP integration.
Symbolized AI’s move from lab experiments to real-world problem solving.
Watson was then applied in:
Healthcare (cancer diagnosis)
Finance (risk management)
Legal services

slides.title: 2. AlphaGo – AI for Strategic Thinking (2016)
slides.text:
2. AlphaGo – AI for Strategic Thinking (2016)
What It Did:
Created by DeepMind (a Google subsidiary).
In 2016, it defeated world champion Lee Sedol in the complex board game Go. Technology Behind AlphaGo:
Combined deep neural networks and reinforcement learning.
Learned by:
Studying millions of expert games • Playing against itself millions of times
Used Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for efficient decision-making. • Impact:
Proved AI could master intuition, not just logic.
Highlighted the power of self-play and generalizable strategy.
Set the foundation for future systems like AlphaZero (trained to master chess, shogi, Go without human input). Legacy:
AlphaGo’s innovations impacted:
Robotics • Game theory • Autonomous systems • Scientific discovery (e.g., AlphaFold for protein folding)

slides.title: 3. GPTs – AI for Language Understanding & Generation (2018–Present)
slides.text:
3. GPTs – AI for Language Understanding & Generation (2018–Present)
What They Do:
Developed by OpenAI, the Generative Pretrained Transformers (GPTs) are large language models that:
Understand and generate human-like text.
Answer questions, write essays, summarize documents, code, and even reason.
Evolution:
GPT-1 (2018) – Proof of concept, small-scale.
GPT-2 (2019) – First widely capable language model; initially withheld over safety concerns.
GPT-3 (2020) – 175B parameters, world’s most powerful LLM at the time.
GPT-4 (2023) – Multimodal; capable of handling images, vision, logic, and nuanced reasoning.
Impact:
GPTs ushered in the generative AI era.
Power tools like:
ChatGPT
Copilot (coding)
DALL·E (images)
Whisper (speech)
Changed education, customer support, research, coding, journalism, and more.

slides.title: Artificial Narrow Intelligence (ANI) – "Weak AI"
slides.text:
Artificial Narrow Intelligence (ANI) – "Weak AI"
Definition: This type of AI is task-specific—designed to perform a single function or a limited range of functions. It can't learn beyond what it's programmed for.
Real-World Examples:
Netflix recommendation system → Suggests shows/movies based on your viewing history using algorithms.
Face recognition apps → Used in smartphones (Face ID), Aadhaar authentication, or security surveillance.
Google Maps / Siri / Alexa → They perform limited but well-defined tasks like navigation or setting reminders.
Spam filters → Recognize patterns to block junk emails.
Key Insight: This is the most common type of AI today—it's everywhere, but it's not truly "intelligent" beyond its coding

slides.title: Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) – "Strong AI"
slides.text:
Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) – "Strong AI"
Definition: AGI refers to machines that can think, reason, learn, and adapt like a human across different domains.
Current Status: We are still developing AGI. Tools like ChatGPT are early examples—they mimic general understanding but lack self-awareness or true reasoning.
Real-World Examples:
OpenAI GPT-4 / GPT-3 / Gemini → Used for general research, tutoring, problem-solving, and coding.
IBM Watson → Used in hospitals and enterprises to analyze medical records or optimize logistics.
AI writing assistants → Tools like Grammarly or Copilot improve human workflows across domains.
Key Insight: We are halfway to AGI. ChatGPT and others showcase multi-domain learning, but don’t yet match full human cognition.

slides.title: Artificial Super Intelligence (ASI) – "Future AI"
slides.text:
Artificial Super Intelligence (ASI) – "Future AI"
Definition: This is hypothetical AI that surpasses human intelligence in every way—logic, creativity, emotions, and decision-making.
Status: Still fictional—has not been achieved.
Imagined Use Cases:
Robots that replace doctors, teachers, judges, etc.
AI that solves complex societal problems (e.g. climate change, space colonization).
Fully autonomous societies run by AI, as seen in sci-fi movies like Her or Ex Machina.
Concerns: Raises ethical and existential risks like job displacement, privacy loss, or AI domination.

slides.title: What is ANI (Artificial Narrow Intelligence)?
slides.text:
What is ANI (Artificial Narrow Intelligence)?
ANI is what we have today. It refers to AI that is designed for a specific task and cannot generalize beyond it. Examples:
Siri and Alexa (voice recognition)
Netflix or Amazon recommendations
Facial recognition systems
Spam filters in email
ANI works only in the domain it was trained for and cannot transfer its skills to unrelated areas

slides.title: How Siri works
slides.text: How Siri works
slides.visual_text: Six-step flow titled How Siri works. Voice Input & Wake Word Detection: microphone continuously listens for the wake word Hey Siri. Speech Recognition (ASR): speech is converted into text using an ASR model. Natural Language Understanding (NLU): text is analyzed to determine intent and parameters. Task Management & Query Resolution: command is routed to the appropriate domain-specific engine. Action Execution: response is generated and action is performed (icon shows 73° on a phone). Feedback Loop & On-Device Learning: utilizes differential privacy to improve through aggregate interactions.

slides.text:
Technical deep dive into how Siri works
1. Voice Input & Wake Word Detection
• Microphone continuously listens for the wake word ("Hey
Siri") using a low-power chip (e.g., Apple's A-series Neural
Engine).
• Uses a wake-word detection model running locally (small
neural network trained to recognize "Hey Siri").
2. Speech Recognition (ASR: Automatic Speech Recognition)
• Once activated, your speech is recorded and processed into
phonemes (basic sound units).
• These are decoded into text using a Recurrent Neural
Network Transducer (RNN-T) or Transformer-based ASR
model.
• This step happens locally or is sent to Apple’s servers
depending on the device's capabilities and settings.
3. Natural Language Understanding (NLU)
• Converts the text into intent + parameters:
• Intent: "get weather"
_
• Parameter: { location: "current", time: "today" }
• Uses models trained with intent classification, slot filling,
and entity recognition (similar to BERT or Apple’s own Core
ML NLP stack). | 4. Task Management & Query Resolution
• The interpreted command is routed to a domain-specific engine:
• E.g., weather, reminders, calendar, phone, or third-party app
integrations via SiriKit.
• These engines call relevant APIs or services (e.g., WeatherKit, Apple Maps,
Contacts).
5. Action Execution
• Based on query results, Siri formats the response:
• Text → Text-to-Speech (TTS)
• Interface → Display info (e.g., weather card)
• TTS is generated using advanced models like WaveNet or Apple’s neural TTS
system for more human-like responses.
6. Feedback Loop & On-Device Learning
• Apple uses differential privacy to learn from aggregate interactions (opt-in).
• Siri adapts through:
• Contextual awareness (location, app usage)
• User preferences (frequently called contacts, typical routes)
• No raw audio is stored; privacy is preserved via on-device learning when
possible.

slides.title: What is AGI (Artificial General Intelligence)?
slides.text:
What is AGI (Artificial General Intelligence)?
AGI, or General AI, refers to an AI system that has human-level intelligence and can perform any intellectual task that a human can. It is:
Flexible: Can learn and apply knowledge across multiple domains
Reasoning-capable: Can solve novel problems, think abstractly, and adapt
Self-improving: Has the ability to learn from experience without being reprogrammed
AGI doesn’t exist yet—it’s a theoretical or future concept. If achieved, it would mark a major shift in how machines interact with the world.

slides.title: Defining AGI: Case Studies
slides.text:
Defining AGI: Case Studies
Explores 9 definitions including:
Turing Test – insufficient, too reliant on deception.
Strong AI (Searle) – requires consciousness, not operationalizable.
Brain Analogy – not necessary for performance.
Cognitive Tasks (Legg, Goertzel) – focuses on capability, not embodiment.
Learning Tasks (Shanahan) – metacognitive ability is key.
Economic Value (OpenAI) – measures usefulness but excludes non-economic intelligence.
Real-world Tasks (Marcus, Suleyman) – emphasizes flexibility and generality.
LLMs as AGI (Arcas & Norvig) – generality present but performance still lacking

slides.title: Six Principles for Defining AGI
slides.text:
Six Principles for Defining AGI
Focus on Capabilities, not Processes (ignore consciousness).
Evaluate Generality and Performance Separately.
Prioritize Cognitive and Metacognitive Tasks (not robotics).
Emphasize Potential, not Deployment.
Ensure Ecological Validity (real-world relevance).
Define Progress as Levels, not a Binary Endpoint.

slides.title: Levels of AGI: The Framework
slides.text:
Levels of AGI: The Framework
A matrix with performance levels (Emerging to Superhuman) × generality (Narrow vs General):
Level 0: No AI (e.g., calculators).
Level 1: Emerging AGI (e.g., ChatGPT).
Level 2: Competent AGI (not yet achieved).
Level 3: Expert AGI.
Level 4: Virtuoso AGI.
Level 5: ASI (Artificial Superintelligence).
Key Idea: AGI is reached not when one task is done superhumanly, but when many are done competently across a range of domains.

Level 5: ASI (Artificial Superintelligence).
Key Idea: AGI is reached not when one task is done superhumanly, but when many are done competently across a range of domains.

slides.title: Testing for AGI
slides.text:
Testing for AGI
Benchmarks Needed: A combination of tasks including cognitive, metacognitive, creative, and social intelligence.
Challenges: Determining which tasks matter, how many to test, and measuring performance ecologically.
Recommendation: Create a living benchmark that evolves and includes real- world tasks with high relevance and diversity.

slides.title: Risk in Context: Autonomy & Human-AI Interaction
slides.text:
Risk in Context: Autonomy & Human-AI Interaction
AGI ≠ Autonomy: Deployment context matters.
Levels of Autonomy (0 to 5):
Tool (basic automation, e.g., grammar checker)
Consultant (AI gives advice when prompted)
Collaborator (shared goals, interactive learning)
Expert (AI leads, human gives feedback)
Agent (fully autonomous AI)
Risk Mapping: Higher AGI + higher autonomy = higher risk (e.g., job displacement, manipulation, misalignment).
Solution: Carefully design human-AI interaction to match the AGI level

slides.title: Conclusion
slides.text:
Conclusion
AGI should be defined based on performance and generality.
The Levels of AGI framework offers a common language to track AI progress and risk.
Benchmarks and interaction paradigms are essential to responsibly develop and deploy AGI.
Calls for collaboration across disciplines to shape the path toward safe AGI

Importance of Internal Control in Business Management 1. Definition and Objectives
IC involves policies and procedures ensuring organizational goals are met.
COSO framework’s five components: Control Environment, Risk Assessment, Control Activities, Information & Communication, and Monitoring. 2. Operational Efficiency
IC ensures tasks are performed consistently.
Reduces waste, rework, and improves customer satisfaction. 3. Risk Management
IC helps identify, assess, and mitigate business risks like fraud or credit risks.
Maintains financial integrity and corporate reputation. 4. Compliance and Governance
IC ensures legal and regulatory compliance.
Supports ethical conduct and accountability through transparent reporting.

slides.visual_text: Figure 14: a timeline showing how AI systems continuously learn and adapt to new business environments and challenges, drawn as rising steps over 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025. Initial Learning (2022): AI starts with basic models and small datasets; it is primarily focused on data collection, basic pattern recognition, and foundational learning algorithms. Continuous Learning (2023): AI adapts based on feedback and new data; the system is refining its models and adjusting based on new inputs, feedback loops, or real-time data. Advanced Learning (2024): AI improves decision-making accuracy and flexibility; more complex algorithms are applied to the data; the system becomes proficient in handling larger datasets and more intricate problems. Mature Learning (2025): AI integrates with complex systems and adapts to dynamic business challenges; at this stage AI is integrated into real-time autonomous decision-making processes, and it can adjust to new and unforeseen challenges with minimal human (intervention; the last word is cut off).

slides.title: What is Artificial Superintelligence (ASI)?
slides.text:
What is Artificial Superintelligence (ASI)?
Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) refers to a hypothetical future AI system that surpasses human intelligence across all domains, including:
Creativity
General wisdom
Scientific reasoning
Emotional intelligence
Strategic decision-making
Social manipulation and persuasion
Whereas AGI (Artificial General Intelligence) matches human-level cognitive capabilities, ASI goes far beyond, potentially becoming the most intelligent entity on Earth

slides.title: Risks and Challenges
slides.text:
Risks and Challenges
1. Alignment Problem
Will ASI share human values? Misaligned goals could lead to catastrophic outcomes. 2. Control Problem
Can we control something vastly more intelligent than us? 3. Existential Risk (X-Risk)
ASI might inadvertently or deliberately harm humanity if misaligned or malicious. 4. Concentration of Power
ASI controlled by a single corporation or government could lead to global inequality or totalitarianism.

Ensures ASI goals are compatible with human values. 2. Interpretability and Explainability
Understanding how ASI reasons and makes decisions.

Institutions like OECD, UN, and partnerships (e.g., Partnership on AI) working on global AI safety protocols. 4. “Boxing” or Constraining ASI
Running ASI in restricted environments to prevent uncontrolled behavior
